messages.author: 484c91357ac83f6b
messages.subject: numerical integration expose gradient
parts:
I tried to use integrate_function in a model and it seems to be working
well, except that it's really slow, making my model unfeasible in practice.

I tracked the bottleneck down to the obvious culprit: the gradient
evaluation... the problem is that we have call var.grad() a really lot
of times to calculate the derivatives.

So the solution I thought of is to allow the user to specify the
derivative of the function to be integrated with respect to each parameter.

So, we would have the simple-to-use version:

integrate_function(function f, real (data only) lower, real
(data only) upper, vector param)

Where f has signature
real function(real x, vector param)

And also the faster version:

integrate_function_grad(function f, function g, real (data only)
lower, real (data only) upper, vector param)

Where f has signature the same signature as before and g
(derivative of f) has signature:
real function(real x, vector param, int n)

Here n tells the function that you want the derivative of f with
respect to param[n].

After I used integrate_function_grad function, the model ran faster by
at least 2 orders of magnitude I think.

However, if I remember well, the idea of exposing the gradient to users
has already been reject a while ago, so I don't know what you think
about this(?)

parts:
Are you integrating the algorithm right now? Or using
the rules that Michael sent?

I don't think something that just computes derivatives
of a simple function is going to provide multiple orders
of magnitude speedup because autodiff isn't that much slower
than analytic derivatives.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] numerical integration expose gradient
parts:
On 08/12/2015 16:51, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Are you integrating the algorithm right now?  Or using
the rules that Michael sent?
Option 2: Using the the rules that Michael sent. I never tried the first.

I don't think something that just computes derivatives
of a simple function is going to provide multiple orders
of magnitude speedup because autodiff isn't that much slower
than analytic derivatives.

In this case, we need to do nested auto-diff a lot of times because we have to integrate x in f(x, param, msgs).grad(); over lower_limit and upper_limit and this must be done again for each element of param (if it's a vector).
